core-concurrency:F1.title: If ffmpeg dies during the start window, the engine stays 'Running' with no capture
core-concurrency:F1.problem: OnProcessExited ignores the exit of a run that is not yet `s.Current` (line 394: "failed during start; StartAsync reports it"). But LaunchRunAsync's poll loop checks `store.Completed.Count > 0` and breaks (line 208) before it checks `run.ExitedTask`. StartAsync then calls AddRun, AfterRunAdded and SetState(Running) (lines 118-122) without checking whether the run has already exited. The janitor watchdog also skips a current run whose ExitedTask is complete (line 415). As a result, no Problem event is raised, the state is never set to Faulted, and nothing detects the problem later.
core-concurrency:F1.failure_scenario: With Resolution=Native, the user alt-tabs out of an exclusive-fullscreen game. The engine faults and the App resumes. The new ddagrab run captures about 1 s, then hits ACCESS_LOST or 'Output parameters changed' because the mode switch is still settling. ffmpeg exits normally and writes the trailer, so the segment muxer lists seg_00000000 in segments.csv. The Exited handler returns early because the run is not current. The next 200 ms poll sees one completed segment, so StartAsync adds the dead run and sets Running. From then on the pill shows REPLAY ON, the App counts CurrentRunUptime >= 20 s as healthy, and nothing more is recorded until the user turns replay off and on. The same happens if ffmpeg dies within about 200 ms after its first segment is listed.
core-concurrency:F1.verified_fix: (1) LaunchRunAsync: check ExitedTask before accepting the first segment: `store.Refresh(); if (run.ExitedTask.IsCompleted) throw StartFailure(run, "ffmpeg stopped right after starting."); if (store.Completed.Count > 0) break;` (optionally keep the store instead of DeleteSession in that case, since the partial segment is valid footage). (2) Close the window between LaunchRunAsync returning and AddRun/SetState: move the body of OnProcessExited into HandleRunExit(Session s, Run run), guarded by a once-only `Interlocked.Exchange(ref run.ExitHandled, 1)`. In OnProcessExited, return without handling while `_state == EngineState.Starting` (StartAsync re-checks). In StartAsync, after `SetState(EngineState.Running)`, add `if (run.ExitedTask.IsCompleted) HandleRunExit(session, run);`. Because MarkExited runs before the state read in OnProcessExited, one of the two paths always sees the exit. Without the Starting guard, an Exited callback that lands between AddRun and SetState(Running) would set Faulted and then be overwritten by Running. (3) Add a backstop in JanitorTick: `if (current is not null && !current.Stopping && current.ExitedTask.IsCompleted && State == EngineState.Running) HandleRunExit(s, current);`.

core-concurrency:F2.title: With audio on, a broken audio pipe hides ffmpeg's real error and always marks the fault as retryable
core-concurrency:F2.problem: When ffmpeg exits on an error, its cleanup closes the audio pipe (ifile_close) before the process ends. The PCM writer then gets a broken pipe, and within about 5 ms the pump's next Write throws, which calls OnPumpFaulted. That sets `run.FaultReason ??= "The audio connection to the video engine broke."` and kills the process. OnProcessExited prefers FaultReason over `Explain(stderr)` and uses `!FaultNotRetryable`, which is true (line 398). So with desktop audio on, which is the default, the message and the retry decision for a mid-run fault often come from this race instead of from ffmpeg's [error] lines.
core-concurrency:F2.failure_scenario: Desktop audio is on. During a UAC prompt ffmpeg logs 'AcquireNextFrame failed: 887a0026', or on a mid-run disk or permission failure it logs 'No space left on device' or 'Permission denied' while opening the next segment. The pump detects the closed pipe before the Exited callback runs. The fault is reported as 'The audio connection to the video engine broke.' and marked retryable. A non-retryable cause (drive full, Controlled Folder Access) is then retried in a loop instead of stopping with 'The buffer drive is full...'. Users and logs see a misleading reason for every crash.
core-concurrency:F2.verified_fix: In OnPumpFaulted, set FaultReason only for faults the pump causes itself: the clock jump, and the sink's 'stopped reading audio for over a minute' overflow. Give these distinct exception types (e.g. AudioClockJumpException in AudioMixerPump, AudioQueueOverflowException in QueuedPcmSink) rather than matching message text. For any other IOException from the sink (broken or closed pipe), keep the Kill but leave FaultReason null, so OnProcessExited uses Explain(run.StderrTail(), code). Optionally, in OnProcessExited, call `run.Process.WaitForExit()` (no timeout, which drains the redirected async stderr) before reading StderrTail, so the [error] lines are present.

core-concurrency:F3.title: Windows Graphics Capture with audio: about 60 s of static screen makes the audio queue overflow and kills the run
core-concurrency:F3.problem: The research (audio-sync.md line 187) says ffmpeg 7+/8's scheduler pauses a stream that is 100 ms or more ahead of the slowest stream. gfxcapture on 8.1-9.1 sends no frames while the screen does not change (video-capture-encoders.md line 338), so the video timestamp stops and the audio demuxer is paused indefinitely. QueuedPcmSink keeps queueing 384 KB/s. At 60 s it sets `_failure` (line 41), the pump faults and OnPumpFaulted kills ffmpeg. The janitor exempts WGC from the stall watchdog because these pauses are expected, but the audio path treats the same pause as fatal.
core-concurrency:F3.failure_scenario: On Windows 11 the user records at 120 fps, so Auto picks WGC (or the App fell back to WGC after two Desktop Duplication failures), with desktop audio on. A paused game, a static loading screen or an AFK menu stays unchanged for 60 s. The audio queue overflows and ffmpeg is killed with 'The audio connection to the video engine broke.' Up to 60 s of queued audio (voice chat, music) is lost. Resume attempts on a static screen then fail with 'No video arrived within 20 seconds', so the buffer keeps restarting with backoff until something on screen moves.
core-concurrency:F3.verified_fix: Preferred: keep WGC video flowing on static screens. Probe gfxcapture for a frame-repeat option (`dup_frames`, present after 9.1) in FfmpegProbe and pass `dup_frames=1` when it exists, as is already done for ddagrab. Without it: (a) do not make the sink overflow fatal for WGC. Use a much larger bound (e.g. 10 min, about 230 MB) or spill the queue to a temp file; do not drop samples, because that would desync audio. (b) In LaunchRunAsync, for Method==WindowsGraphicsCapture, treat 'process alive and -progress frame>0' as started instead of requiring a completed segment, so a static screen does not cause the 20 s fail/backoff loop. (c) If overflow still ends a run, give it its own reason (e.g. 'Nothing changed on screen for a minute; capture restarted') and do not count it toward the backoff streak.

core-concurrency:F4.title: An automatic resume at a new display mode deletes the entire replay buffer
core-concurrency:F4.problem: Before each resume the App re-enumerates monitors and resolves Native size and EffectiveFps from the current mode, so the new run's Signature (encoder|WxH|fps|audio) changes. Two seconds later the janitor calls DeleteExpired(-inf) on every run that is not compatible with the newest one, then removes those runs and their folders. This goes against SPEC 'The engine keeps the buffer across restarts' and against the research recommendation (video-capture-encoders.md line 511): 'Resolution can change after a restart, so always scale to a fixed output size ... or never concat across runs'. The code chose not to concat across runs, but it also deletes those runs.
core-concurrency:F4.failure_scenario: A CS2 player runs exclusive fullscreen at 1280x960 on a 2560x1440 monitor, with the default Resolution=Native, and has 30 minutes of gameplay in the buffer. They alt-tab to PC Clipper to press 'Save last 5 min'. The mode switch causes 'Output parameters changed', and the App resumes at 2560x1440, which is a new signature. About 2 s after the new run starts, the janitor deletes all 30 minutes of gameplay. The save then contains only the few seconds since the switch, with no warning. The same happens when the refresh rate change alters EffectiveFps.
core-concurrency:F4.verified_fix: For keepBuffer resumes, hold the output format fixed. In AppController.StartReplayAsync, when kind==Resume, `_engine.ActiveConfig` is non-null and the user's capture settings have not changed, build cfg for the current monitor and then override Width, Height, Fps, Vendor, Codec, EncoderName and BitrateKbps from ActiveConfig via cfg.With(...). VideoGraph already inserts scale_d3d11 (NVIDIA/AMD/CPU) whenever cfg.Width/Height differ from cfg.Monitor, and the Intel path always runs vpp_qsv, so the new run stays signature-compatible and saves keep joining across the switch. In addition, change the janitor so incompatible runs are not deleted with -inf: keep them until they fall outside BufferSeconds measured across all runs. Optionally let SaveLastAsync fall back to the newest compatible group and warn that an earlier part was recorded at a different size.

core-concurrency:F5.title: A recording restarted after an incompatible restart is missing footage, and can restart after the user stopped it
core-concurrency:F5.problem: When a run with a different signature is added during a recording, AfterRunAdded starts a background task that first saves the old part with FinishRecordingIfAnyAsync. That save waits up to 7 s in WaitForCurrentSegmentAsync on the new run and then concatenates the whole recording so far, which can take seconds to minutes. Only after that does it call StartRecording(), which pins from the run's CurrentWritingIndex at that later moment instead of index 0. The new run's footage from the restart until then is in neither recording. While the old part is saving, _recording is null, so the UI shows 'not recording' and a user Stop returns 'Not recording.' The task then calls StartRecording() unconditionally, so a recording starts again even though the user pressed Stop.
core-concurrency:F5.failure_scenario: The user records for 20 minutes, the game changes display mode and the resume runs at a new size. Saving the 20-minute part takes about 40 s. Recording part 2 starts about 45 s into the new run, so those 45 s are missing from the recording even though the user never stopped it. If the user presses Stop during those 45 s, they get 'Not recording', and then a new recording starts anyway.
core-concurrency:F5.verified_fix: In AfterRunAdded, swap the recording atomically: `Recording? old; lock (_gate) { old = _recording; if (old is null) return; _recording = new Recording(run, 0); }` (pins the new run from index 0, so nothing is lost and IsRecording stays true). Then save the detached `old` in the background with a variant of StopRecordingAsync that takes the Recording and the Session and skips WaitForCurrentSegmentAsync (the old runs are finished). Raise RecordingAutoSaved with the result. Remove the later StartRecording() call, so a user Stop issued meanwhile simply stops the new part. Optionally carry the old Clock's start time over, so RecordingElapsed and the App's file name stay sensible.

core-concurrency:F6.title: The stall watchdog misses new segments found by other code and kills a healthy ffmpeg
core-concurrency:F6.problem: The watchdog updates LastNewSegmentUtc only when the janitor's own Refresh changes CurrentWritingIndex. WaitForCurrentSegmentAsync (saves, stop recording) and StartRecording also call Refresh, polling every 100 ms. Each save's polling ends exactly when a new segment appears, so that save, not the janitor, sees the change. With queued saves running back to back, every new segment is seen by a save, and after 15 s (stallLimit = max(15, 6*2)) the janitor kills ffmpeg.
core-concurrency:F6.failure_scenario: The user presses the 'save 15 s' hotkey or tray item 8 times quickly (saves queue, as SPEC requires). Each save waits for the next segment (about 2 s) and its concat takes about 0.2 s, so for about 16 s the janitor never sees CurrentWritingIndex change. It kills a healthy ffmpeg with 'Screen capture froze (no new video for 15 seconds)', loses the segment being written and forces a restart.
core-concurrency:F6.verified_fix: Track freshness in SegmentStore: add `public DateTime LastNewSegmentUtc { get; private set; } = DateTime.UtcNow;`, set under _gate in Refresh whenever `_known.Add(seg.Index)` succeeds. In JanitorTick, drop the before/after comparison and use `var last = current.Store.LastNewSegmentUtc > current.LastNewSegmentUtc ? current.Store.LastNewSegmentUtc : current.LastNewSegmentUtc; if (Method==DesktopDuplication && DateTime.UtcNow - last > stallLimit) ...`.

core-concurrency:F7.title: Teardown deletes the buffer folder after 2 minutes even if a save is still copying
core-concurrency:F7.problem: SPEC says to delete the session folder after any in-flight save finishes. TearDownSessionAsync waits at most 2 minutes for ActiveOps to reach zero (lines 341-343), then deletes the folder, while ConcatAsync allows a save to run for 40 minutes. On Windows, MPEG-TS saves survive because concatf opens all segments up front and open files cannot be deleted. AV1 saves use the concat demuxer, which opens each .mkv only when it reaches it, so segments it has not opened yet are deleted.
core-concurrency:F7.failure_scenario: An AV1 (av1_nvenc) user saves 'last 1 hour' at 4K, which is tens of GB and takes several minutes on an HDD, then clicks Turn OFF or applies new settings. After 2 minutes teardown deletes the remaining .mkv segments. The concat demuxer fails to open the next file, so the save fails ('Saving failed...') or produces a truncated clip, and the clip the user asked for is lost.
core-concurrency:F7.verified_fix: Do not time-limit the wait, or hand the deletion to the last operation: add `bool TornDown` on Session. In TearDownSessionAsync, set TornDown=true, then `if (Volatile.Read(ref s.ActiveOps) == 0 && Interlocked.Exchange(ref s.Deleted, 1) == 0) DeleteDirectory(s.Dir);`. In the finally blocks of SaveLastAsync and StopRecordingAsync, `if (Interlocked.Decrement(ref s.ActiveOps) == 0 && s.TornDown && Interlocked.Exchange(ref s.Deleted, 1) == 0) DeleteDirectory(s.Dir);`. The Interlocked handshake ensures exactly one deletion. Teardown then never deletes files a running save still needs. Stale folders are already cleaned at the next start.

ffmpeg-correctness:F1.title: A failed recording save deletes the recording; very long recordings can never be saved
ffmpeg-correctness:F1.problem: StopRecordingAsync always calls rec.Dispose() in its finally block. That drops the PinFrom pins whether ConcatAsync succeeded or not. On the next janitor tick (2 s), DeleteExpired removes every segment older than BufferSeconds+4 s. On StopAsync or exit, FinishRecordingIfAnyAsync is followed by TearDownSessionAsync, which deletes the whole session folder anyway. Long recordings also fail for certain. The concatf protocol (concat.c concatf_open) opens every listed segment up front and keeps them all open. Each one is a CRT descriptor (file protocol → _wsopen). Both pinned builds link the UCRT (they import api-ms-win-crt-*), which caps lowio descriptors at 8192. On top of that, the save has a fixed 40-minute timeout (line 712). The Linux research run passed with 1800 files only because its ulimit was 20000.
ffmpeg-correctness:F1.failure_scenario: Case 1: the user records a 2-hour session and presses Stop while the clips drive is nearly full. ffmpeg fails with 'No space left', the toast says 'the clips drive is full', and 2 s later the janitor deletes everything older than the buffer window, although the segments were safe on the buffer drive. Case 2: a recording longer than about 4.5 h (more than 8190 two-second segments) fails with 'Too many open files' and is lost the same way. Case 3: a multi-hour 5K recording on an HDD takes more than 40 min to copy, times out, and is lost. SPEC promises that recording length is unlimited and that a recording is never lost.
ffmpeg-correctness:F1.verified_fix: (1) In StopRecordingAsync, dispose the Recording's pins only when ConcatAsync succeeded. On failure, move the Recording into a _pendingRecordings list. It stays pinned and is no longer the active recording. Add RetryPendingRecordingAsync(path), and have AppController offer it (Retry / pick another folder), or retry automatically once space is free. (2) TearDownSessionAsync and the StartAsync(keepBuffer:false) path must not delete s.Dir while pending recordings exist. Either keep that session folder (skip CleanupStaleSessions for it) or, as a last resort, save the recording to the buffer drive (e.g. <BufferRoot>/Recovered Recording ...mp4) before releasing the pins. (3) In ConcatAsync, split each run's segments into chunks of 1000 or fewer. Write one concatf list per chunk, then one ffconcat that lists 'file concatf:...' per chunk, the same way multi-run saves already work. The concat demuxer opens one chunk at a time, so the descriptor count stays bounded. (4) Scale the save timeout with the input size, e.g. max(40 min, totalBytes / (15 MB/s)), and count segment bytes from the store.

ffmpeg-correctness:F2.title: An encoder on a different GPU than the monitor's is chosen, but the capture chain only works on the monitor's GPU
ffmpeg-correctness:F2.problem: ResolveVendor accepts any vendor whose encoder passed the probe, both for an explicit choice (line 140) and in the Auto fallback loop (line 150). The probe encodes system-memory NV12, so it passes on any GPU in the PC. VideoGraph, however, always builds a zero-copy graph on the D3D11 device of the monitor's adapter (AddHwDevice, FfmpegCommandBuilder.cs:94): NVENC and AMF take ddagrab's D3D11 frames directly, and QSV uses hwmap derive_device from that device. Each encoder opens on the frames' device. The research gives a cross-GPU recipe (-init_hw_device cuda + hwdownload), but nothing implements it, and Warnings() says nothing. ReplayEngine.Explain (line 838) then maps NVENC's 'OpenEncodeSessionEx failed: unsupported device' to 'encoder is busy, close OBS/Discord' and marks it retryable.
ffmpeg-correctness:F2.failure_scenario: On an Optimus or Ryzen+RTX laptop in hybrid mode, the internal panel belongs to the iGPU (AdapterIndex 0). The user picks Encoder = NVIDIA. h264_nvenc passed the probe, so the command uses -init_hw_device d3d11va=dda:0 with hevc_nvenc fed Intel/AMD D3D11 textures, and nvEncOpenEncodeSessionEx fails. The app retries 6 times, then shows 'NVIDIA encoder is busy... close other recorders'. The same happens in Auto mode when the monitor GPU's encoder fails the probe and the loop falls back to another adapter's NVENC, AMF or QSV, for example on an Intel+NVIDIA desktop with an NVIDIA driver older than 570.
ffmpeg-correctness:F2.verified_fix: Determine the monitor's vendor (MonitorInfo.GpuVendorId). In ResolveVendor, when a hardware vendor other than the monitor GPU's vendor would be chosen (explicitly or by the Auto loop), either: (a) emit a cross-adapter graph. For NVENC that is: add '-init_hw_device cuda=nv' and, in VideoGraph, 'scale_d3d11=...:format=nv12,hwdownload,format=nv12' (or 'hwdownload,format=bgra') before the encoder, so it gets system-memory frames. Do the same hwdownload path for AMF and QSV. Or (b) do not choose it: fall back to the monitor GPU's encoder, else CPU, and add a Warnings() line such as 'This screen is connected to the <Intel> graphics chip; the NVIDIA encoder can't record it directly - using X'. In Explain, check 'unsupported device' / 'no encode device' (and AMF 'given D3D11 device' failures) before the OpenEncodeSessionEx 'busy' rule, and return a non-retryable 'screen is connected to another graphics chip' message.

ffmpeg-correctness:F3.title: Windows Graphics Capture on a still screen: start times out, audio overflows, and a burst of duplicate frames follows
ffmpeg-correctness:F3.problem: gfxcapture in 8.1 sends frames only when the screen changes (vsrc_gfxcapture_winrt.cpp activate waits on FrameArrived and has no dup_frames). The fps filter (line 120) needs the next input frame before it outputs anything. Three things then go wrong. (a) LaunchRunAsync (ReplayEngine.cs:208) counts the run as running only when the first segment closes, which never happens on a still desktop, so it fails after 20 s with 'No video arrived'. (b) While running, the scheduler holds back the audio input once it is 100 ms (SCHEDULE_TOLERANCE) ahead of the stalled video. QueuedPcmSink then hits its 60-s limit, the pump faults, and the run is killed. The restart fails as in (a). AppController only falls back from WGC to DDA when WGC was an override, not when Auto resolved to WGC (QualityMath.cs:229). (c) When the screen changes again, vf_fps fills the whole gap with duplicates in one burst (40 s × 120 = 4800 frames). gfxcapture's 2-frame pool drops the live frames meanwhile, so the first seconds of renewed action are frozen.
ffmpeg-correctness:F3.failure_scenario: On Windows 11 with a 144 Hz monitor, fps 120 and capture method Auto, the app uses WGC. With 'Start with Windows' and 'Turn replay on when PC Clipper starts' (the default), the desktop is idle after login. Each start waits 20 s; after 6 attempts the replay turns OFF with 'Replay couldn't start: The video engine stopped unexpectedly'. Later, while the user is AFK on the desktop for more than a minute, capture cycles through fault and restart ('Capture interrupted — resuming…'), and up to 30 s of backoff can miss the start of the next game.
ffmpeg-correctness:F3.verified_fix: (1) LaunchRunAsync: for CaptureMethod.WindowsGraphicsCapture, consider the run started once the anchor line has arrived (setpts prints it for the first captured frame, which WGC delivers at session start) and ffmpeg is still alive about 2 s later. Do not require a completed segment. Note that 'frame>0' from -progress would NOT work, because vf_fps holds the single frame back. (2) AppController.MaybeSwitchCaptureMethod: when _settings.CaptureMethod == Auto and _lastMethod == WindowsGraphicsCapture (whether chosen by Auto or by the override), set _methodOverride = CaptureMethod.DesktopDuplication after quick failures, and let BuildConfig apply it. (3) Avoid the audio overflow under WGC. Prefer Auto = DDA unless Test my PC actually measured the ~64 fps cap, or use WGC only when the user forces it. Alternatively treat an overflow while the WGC video is known to be stalled as 'pause' rather than a fault, e.g. raise the cap and log instead of killing. Only FFmpeg after 9.1 has gfxcapture dup_frames.

ffmpeg-correctness:F4.title: Test my PC reports 'Too heavy' because its speed and fps include fixed startup and shutdown time
ffmpeg-correctness:F4.problem: speed and fps are read from the final '-progress' block. ffmpeg computes them over the wall time from just after sch_start to after sch_stop and the trailer (fftools/ffmpeg.c transcode/print_report). That window includes configuring the source filter (DuplicateOutput1 or WGC session creation, QSV session) and closing the encoder (NVENC/AMF destroy). out_time is the last frame's pts (5 − 1/F). With 5-s runs, speed ≥ 0.97 tolerates only about 120–145 ms of total fixed overhead (4.983/0.97 = 5.137 s at 60 fps), and fps ≥ 0.95F about 260 ms. Even a cheap realtime testsrc2 plus x264 run on this machine's ffmpeg already reports speed=0.989x.
ffmpeg-correctness:F4.failure_scenario: A PC whose NVENC easily keeps up at 1440p60 spends about 80 ms on D3D11 duplication setup and about 100 ms on NVENC/CUDA teardown. The result is speed ≈ 0.965, and the user sees 'Too heavy: the encoder only reached 58.9 fps (speed 0.97x)… Try a lower resolution or frame rate'. The message even prints a speed that looks like it passes. Users lower their quality for no reason, and the test that is supposed to back up the accepted ~64 fps DDA risk gives wrong answers.
ffmpeg-correctness:F4.verified_fix: Measure only the steady-state window. Give FfmpegRunner.RunAsync an optional per-line stdout callback, or stream the progress lines. Record a Stopwatch timestamp when each 'progress=continue' block completes. Compute speed = Δout_time_us / Δwall and fps = Δframe / Δwall between the first block at ≥1 s and the last 'continue' block before 'end'. Run 6-7 s so at least 4 periodic blocks fall inside the window. Keep the 0.97 / 0.95 thresholds for that window only, and print the speed with three decimals, or print the threshold, so the message is not self-contradictory.

ffmpeg-correctness:F5.title: CPU fallback picks libx265 with no resolution or frame-rate cap, so the encoder cannot keep up
ffmpeg-correctness:F5.problem: ResolveCodec tries HEVC first for every vendor. For EncoderVendor.Cpu, 'works' only means compiled in, and libx265 is in both pinned builds. So whenever no GPU encoder works, Auto codec becomes libx265 -preset veryfast, several times slower than libx264 veryfast, which the research recommends for CPU. Resolve (line 240) caps the size only for hardware H.264, never for CPU. When the encoder is slower than real time, ddagrab is not polled. vf_fps then fills each gap with duplicates, so the time between ddagrab polls grows every cycle, the video turns into long frozen stretches, and the scheduler holds back the audio pipe until QueuedPcmSink overflows. Warnings() only says 'will very likely stutter'.
ffmpeg-correctness:F5.failure_scenario: An NVIDIA driver older than 570 (common on OEM laptops) makes every NVENC probe fail. Vendor Auto resolves to CPU and codec Auto to libx265 at the native 2560x1440@60. While a game runs, x265 manages about 30–40 fps. The clips freeze for seconds at a time, the game slows down, and about every few minutes 'The audio connection to the video engine broke' triggers a restart.
ffmpeg-correctness:F5.verified_fix: In ResolveCodec, when vendor == EncoderVendor.Cpu and requested == VideoCodec.Auto, try H264 first (libx264 handles >4096 widths too), and use Hevc only when explicitly requested. For example: var order = vendor == EncoderVendor.Cpu ? new[]{H264, Hevc, Av1} : new[]{Hevc, H264, Av1}; and drop the width>4096 exclusion of H.264 for the CPU vendor. Optionally, when Vendor resolves to Cpu with Auto settings, cap the resolved size and frame rate (e.g. 1080p60) and add a Warnings() line saying so.

ffmpeg-correctness:F6.title: H.264 fallback above 4096 px wide does not reduce the width on ultrawide monitors
ffmpeg-correctness:F6.problem: When hardware H.264 is the only codec left and w > 4096, Resolve calls TargetSize(P2160, monitor). TargetSize keeps the monitor's aspect ratio and returns the native size when nativeHeight == 2160. For 5120x2160 the width stays 5120. For 32:9 5120x1440 it becomes 7680x2160, which is upscaled and even wider. The research specifically flags 5120x1440 and 5120x2160 as over the H.264 limit.
ffmpeg-correctness:F6.failure_scenario: A 5120x1440 monitor on a GPU whose HEVC/AV1 probe failed (H.264-only GPUs such as NVIDIA Kepler or Maxwell-1, AMD VCE1/2, or an HEVC probe that failed because a session was busy) resolves to h264 at 7680x2160. The encoder fails with 'Width 7680 exceeds 4096' and replay cannot start.
ffmpeg-correctness:F6.verified_fix: Replace the cap with a width-based one: if (codec == H264 && vendor != Cpu && (w > 4096 || h > 4096)) { double k = Math.Min(4096.0 / w, 4096.0 / h); w = Even((int)Math.Floor(w * k)); h = Even((int)Math.Floor(h * k)); clamp each to ≤ 4096 }. Use floor or round-down-to-even so Even() cannot push past 4096. Apply the same width/height rule in ResolveCodec's Ok() and the SettingsView label so the UI matches.

ffmpeg-correctness:F7.title: Rotated (portrait) monitors are recorded and screenshotted sideways or stretched
ffmpeg-correctness:F7.problem: ddagrab sizes its output from the duplicated desktop texture (vsrc_ddagrab.c sets raw_width/width from desc.Width), which comes in the unrotated orientation. It rotates only the mouse coordinates (lines 608-618). MonitorInfo.Width/Height come from DesktopCoordinates, which are rotated. DxgiMonitors reads DXGI_OUTPUT_DESC.Rotation but throws it away, so VideoGraph, ResolveMethod and BuildScreenshotArgs (line 299) never compensate. The research already said to use gfxcapture for portrait monitors.
ffmpeg-correctness:F7.failure_scenario: The user records a 1440x2560 portrait monitor. At Native, cfg 1440x2560 equals the Monitor size, so there is no scaling and NVENC encodes a 2560x1440 sideways picture. With the 1080p preset, scale_d3d11 or vpp_qsv squeezes the sideways 2560x1440 image into 608x1080. Screenshots of that monitor are sideways as well.
ffmpeg-correctness:F7.verified_fix: Read od.Rotation in DxgiMonitors.EnumerateDxgi and add a Rotation property to MonitorInfo (DXGI_MODE_ROTATION: 2 = 90, 3 = 180, 4 = 270). For rotated outputs, prefer gfxcapture in ResolveMethod when it is available, since WGC delivers the upright image. Otherwise, with DDA: compute the 'scale' check and scaler input against the unrotated size, then rotate. On the CPU path, add 'transpose=clock|cclock' (or 'hflip,vflip' for 180°) after hwdownload,format=nv12. On QSV, use vpp_qsv's transpose option. For NVENC/AMF there is no D3D11 transpose filter in 8.1, so use hwdownload + transpose and feed system-memory frames, or force WGC. In BuildScreenshotArgs, add the same transpose after 'hwdownload,format=bgra'. Verify the clock/cclock direction for ROTATE90 vs ROTATE270 on real hardware.

windows-interop:F1.title: Every launch silently turns autostart back on after the user disables it in Task Manager
windows-interop:F1.problem: Apply(true) always deletes PC Clipper's StartupApproved\Run value, which is the flag Task Manager and Settings > Startup apps use to mark an entry as disabled. AppController.LoadSettings (AppController.cs:455-459) calls Apply(true) on every launch whenever settings.StartWithWindows is true. That call was meant only to refresh the exe path, but it also erases the user's 'Disabled' choice. StartupRegistration.IsEnabled(), written to read the real state, is never called anywhere. The Settings checkbox (SettingsView.cs:499) shows the stored setting, so it keeps showing 'Start with Windows' as on.
windows-interop:F1.failure_scenario: The user disables 'PC Clipper' in Task Manager > Startup apps, which writes 03 00.. under HKCU\...\Explorer\StartupApproved\Run. Later they open PC Clipper from the Start menu. LoadSettings -> Apply(true) -> approved.DeleteValue("PC Clipper") runs. On the next boot PC Clipper starts with Windows again (and turns the replay buffer on if that setting is set). This repeats every time they open the app, and the Settings page never shows that autostart was off.
windows-interop:F1.verified_fix: 1) Add StartupRegistration.RefreshPath(): open the Run key, and only if the value exists as a string that differs from Command, SetValue(Command). It must never touch StartupApproved. 2) In LoadSettings, replace Apply(true) with: if (s.StartWithWindows) { if (StartupRegistration.IsEnabled()) RefreshPath(); else s.StartWithWindows = false; }, then log it. This handles both a Task Manager disable and a cleaner deleting the Run value, and the checkbox then shows the real state. 3) Delete the StartupApproved value only in the user-initiated path (AppController.cs:1508-1510, old != new with new == true). The simplest way is to keep Apply(bool) for that path and use RefreshPath at startup. Optionally re-read IsEnabled() when the Settings page opens, so a Task Manager change made while the app runs also shows up.

windows-interop:F2.title: Shutdown while recording loses the recording when the window was never opened (SessionEnding runs on the UI thread and does not block)
windows-interop:F2.problem: SystemEvents is first used on the STA UI thread (the AppController constructor and WinForms itself). SystemEvents then shares that thread, so SessionEnding (WM_QUERYENDSESSION) is raised on the UI thread. OnSessionEnding handles that case by calling OnWindowsShutdown() and returning straight away. That call only starts ExitAsync as fire-and-forget async; e.Cancel is not set and nothing waits. The comment 'Raised on the system-events thread (never the UI thread...)' gets the threading backwards. The 6-second wait only exists in the branch that never runs. The only other protection is MainForm.OnFormClosing, which sets e.Cancel while recording, but it only applies if MainForm has a window handle. With --minimized (Start with Windows) the form is constructed but never shown, so it has no handle and never receives WM_QUERYENDSESSION. The hotkey window is message-only and gets no broadcasts. The toast form closes without cancelling.
windows-interop:F2.failure_scenario: PC Clipper autostarts minimized to the tray. In a game the user presses the record hotkey and records for 20 minutes, then shuts Windows down without stopping. WM_QUERYENDSESSION returns TRUE at once. ExitAsync has only started FinishRecordingAsync on the thread pool when WM_ENDSESSION arrives and the process is terminated. The job object kills the concat ffmpeg, leaving a .part.mp4. On the next start, CleanupStaleBufferAsync deletes the session folder that held the segments. The recording is lost for good. SPEC requires 'same as exit, best effort within a few seconds'.
windows-interop:F2.verified_fix: 1) In the AppController constructor, right after `_form = new MainForm(this);`, add `_ = _form.Handle;`. This creates the hidden top-level HWND without showing the form, so MainForm.OnFormClosing always receives CloseReason.WindowsShutDown and cancels while recording. 2) In OnSessionEnding's UI-thread branch, set `e.Cancel = _engine.IsRecording || _recordingSaving;` before calling OnWindowsShutdown(), so the SystemEvents window also returns FALSE. 3) When cancelling, call ShutdownBlockReasonCreate(_form.Handle, "Saving your recording") (user32, CharSet.Unicode, SetLastError). Call ShutdownBlockReasonDestroy in Shutdown(). 4) In ExitAsync, when the shutdown was blocked to protect a recording, don't use the 4 s cap. Wait for FinishRecordingAsync with a generous limit (for example 60-120 s; Windows shows its 'Shut down anyway' screen meanwhile) before StopAsync/Shutdown. Otherwise ExitThread plus the job object kill the concat anyway. 5) Fix the comment at :1837 to say that SystemEvents normally runs on this STA UI thread here.

windows-interop:F3.title: 'Default microphone' records the Default Communications device, not the Windows default recording device
windows-interop:F3.problem: When no microphone is chosen (the 'Default microphone' entry, id null), ResolveDevice uses GetDefaultAudioEndpoint(Capture, Role.Communications). Default-device change tracking (line 397) and the 'default' mark in AudioDevices.Microphones (AudioDevices.cs:25-27) also use the Communications role. Windows keeps two separate recording defaults: 'Default Device' (eConsole/eMultimedia, the one most recorders such as OBS use) and 'Default Communication Device' (meant for VoIP apps). They are often different devices.
windows-interop:F3.failure_scenario: A user has a USB headset mic set as the Windows 'Default Device' and a webcam mic that is still the 'Default Communication Device'. This is common after right-click > 'Set as Default Device' in the Sound control panel, which only changes the console/multimedia roles. They tick 'Record microphone' and keep 'Default microphone'. PC Clipper records the webcam mic, and the Settings list also marks the webcam as the default. Changing the 'Default Device' in Windows has no effect either.
windows-interop:F3.verified_fix: Change Role.Communications to Role.Console in the HasDefaultAudioEndpoint/GetDefaultAudioEndpoint calls in WasapiAudioSource.ResolveDevice (:249, :251), in AudioDevices.Microphones (:25, :27), and in the OnDefaultDeviceChanged filter (`flow == DataFlow.Capture && role == Role.Console`, :397). Windows raises OnDefaultDeviceChanged once per role, so filtering on Console is enough. Update the doc comments at WasapiAudioSource.cs:22, AudioDevices.cs:12 and AppSettings.cs:61 to match.

ui-controller:F1.title: Supervised resume rebuilds the capture config from the current display mode, so the whole replay buffer is deleted after a fullscreen mode switch
ui-controller:F1.problem: StartReplayAsync re-enumerates monitors before every start (line 795). For StartKind.Resume it then calls BuildConfig(caps, _settings) → QualityMath.Resolve with the monitor's current mode. With the default Resolution=Native, TargetSize returns the monitor's current size. EffectiveFps uses the current refresh rate, and ResolveVendor uses the current adapter. If any of these changed, the new run gets a different CaptureConfig.Signature (EncoderName|WxH|Fps|audio). In the engine, CompatibleRunsNewestFirst() then drops every older run, and on its next 2 s tick JanitorTick calls DeleteExpired(double.NegativeInfinity) on all of their segments. SaveLastAsync and Buffered also only look at compatible runs. keepBuffer:true therefore does nothing in exactly the case the SPEC names as the reason for supervision ("UAC prompts / fullscreen switches cause these"). The user gets no message about it.
ui-controller:F1.failure_scenario: A user on a 2560x1440 desktop with default settings plays an exclusive-fullscreen game at 1920x1080 (for example CS2 at a stretched resolution). Alt-tabbing or quitting to the desktop switches the mode back, ddagrab loses access, and the engine faults (retryable). The resume resolves 2560x1440, the signature changes, and within 2 s the janitor deletes the game run's segments. The user presses "Save last 15 min" and gets only the few seconds since the desktop came back. The same happens with 120 fps settings when a game drops the display to 60 Hz, and on hybrid-graphics laptops when fullscreen moves the display from the iGPU to the dGPU (the vendor or encoder changes).
ui-controller:F1.verified_fix: In StartReplayAsync, for StartKind.Resume with _engine.ActiveConfig != null (the faulted run's config is still the session's Current), build cfg from the new monitor (cfg.Monitor must be the new MonitorInfo/HMONITOR) but carry over prev.Width/Height/Fps/BitrateKbps. Also keep prev.Vendor/Codec/EncoderName/MinimalEncoderFlags when the new monitor's GpuVendorId still maps to that vendor and caps.Works(prev.EncoderName). Add settable Width/Height/BitrateKbps to CaptureConfigBuilder: Build() currently copies _src.Width/_src.Height. FfmpegCommandBuilder:122 already inserts scale_d3d11/vpp_qsv when cfg.Width != cfg.Monitor.Width, so the signature stays equal and the runs join. Only when the signature really must change (different adapter) should JanitorTick stop wiping incompatible runs immediately: keep them while they are inside BufferSeconds and let SaveLastAsync save the newest incompatible run as a separate file. Either way, notify the user ("Display changed - the replay continues; earlier footage was kept/saved separately").

ui-controller:F2.title: On Windows shutdown the window blocks shutdown to protect a recording, then ExitAsync gives up after 4 s and the recording is lost
ui-controller:F2.problem: MainForm.OnFormClosing (MainForm.cs:273-276) sets e.Cancel = true while recording or saving a recording, which makes WM_QUERYENDSESSION return FALSE and holds Windows on the "PC Clipper is preventing shutdown" screen. ExitAsync(sessionEnding: true) then waits only 4 s for FinishRecordingAsync (line 1783) and 3 s for StopAsync before calling Shutdown(), which exits the process. The concat ffmpeg is attached to the kill-on-close job object (FfmpegRunner guard), so it is killed mid-write and leaves only '<name>.mp4.part'. The unsaved segments are in the session folder, which CleanupStaleBufferAsync deletes on the next launch. Blocking shutdown buys time, but the time is then thrown away.
ui-controller:F2.failure_scenario: A user records a 10-minute session (about 3 GB at the default ~39 Mbps; ≤10 min also gets +faststart, which rewrites the file) and shuts the PC down without pressing Stop. WaitForCurrentSegmentAsync plus the stream copy take well over 4 s on a SATA SSD or HDD. ExitAsync times out, the process exits, the job object kills ffmpeg, and the recording is gone. The next start deletes the leftover segments too.
ui-controller:F2.verified_fix: While the form has cancelled WM_QUERYENDSESSION for a recording, call ShutdownBlockReasonCreate(Handle, "Saving your recording...") (user32, CharSet.Unicode). In ExitAsync(sessionEnding:true), await the recording save task with a much longer limit (for example the same 10 min as a normal exit, or until done), since Windows only proceeds when the user clicks 'Shut down anyway' or the process exits. Then call ShutdownBlockReasonDestroy(Handle) before Shutdown(). Keep the 3 s StopAsync cap only after the save has completed. Update SPEC:241 to match.

ui-controller:F3.title: Exit and shutdown ignore in-flight "Save the last…" clips; capped timeouts kill the concat ffmpeg and the clip is lost
ui-controller:F3.problem: ExitAsync only waits for manual recordings (`_engine.IsRecording || _recordingSaving`). A clip save in _savesInFlight is never awaited. The engine's StopAsync would wait up to 2 minutes for ActiveOps, but the app wraps it in WithTimeout of 30 s (3 s at shutdown, line 1787) and then calls Shutdown(). Process exit closes the job object and kills the concat ffmpeg. MainForm.OnFormClosing (MainForm.cs:273) also only blocks shutdown for recordings, not clip saves. The 10-minute limit on recording saves at normal exit (line 1783) has the same outcome for very long recordings.
ui-controller:F3.failure_scenario: A user presses "Save the last 1 hour" (about 17.6 GB at default settings) and then chooses Exit from the tray, or shuts the PC down for the night. The stream copy takes longer than 30 s on a SATA SSD or HDD (or 3 s at shutdown). PC Clipper exits, the job object kills ffmpeg, the clips folder keeps a useless 'Clip ... .mp4.part', and the next launch deletes the buffer. The user never got a "Saved" toast and only notices later that the clip is missing. Likewise, a 3-hour recording (~50 GB) saved on exit to an HDD is killed after 10 minutes.
ui-controller:F3.verified_fix: Keep a HashSet<Task> _clipSaveTasks: add the task in SaveLastAsync and remove it on completion, and expose IsAnySaveInFlight. In ExitAsync, before StopAsync, if any clip or recording save is in flight, ShowBusyNotice("Saving your clip before closing...") (plus a toast when hidden) and await Task.WhenAll(saves) with no 30 s/10 min cap on a normal exit. Apply the 30 s cap only to StopAsync after the saves have completed. In MainForm.OnFormClosing, include IsAnySaveInFlight in protectRecording for WindowsShutDown and pair it with ShutdownBlockReasonCreate/Destroy (see F2).

ui-controller:F4.title: Automatic Windows Graphics Capture fallback stays on for the whole session and ignores Windows 10's yellow border
ui-controller:F4.problem: MaybeSwitchCaptureMethod sets _methodOverride = WindowsGraphicsCapture after 2 quick Desktop Duplication failures, checking only WgcPossible (gfxcapture present and HMONITOR known, line 906). There is no Windows 11 check, although the SPEC's own Auto rule limits WGC to Windows 11 because of the border. SuperviseTick (lines 1121-1131) resets the fail counters after a healthy run but never clears _methodOverride, so BuildConfig (line 891) keeps forcing WGC on every later restart until the user turns the replay off.
ui-controller:F4.failure_scenario: A Windows 10 user starts a game installer and its UAC prompt stays up for about 5 s. Two restart attempts fail on the secure desktop (_methodQuickFails reaches 2), the override switches to WGC, and capture resumes after the prompt. For the rest of the evening a yellow capture border surrounds the screen. Because WGC pauses on static screens, saves of quiet moments come out shorter. The non-technical user has no idea why the border appeared or how to remove it.
ui-controller:F4.verified_fix: In MaybeSwitchCaptureMethod, require QualityMath.IsWindows11 for the automatic switch, or on Windows 10 notify the user once that a yellow border will appear and how to avoid it. In SuperviseTick's healthy-run branch (and/or in RegisterFailure when healthy), set _methodOverride = null so the next interruption tries Desktop Duplication first and the fallback really covers only the restart(s) that needed it.

ui-controller:F5.title: "Stop download" closes the whole FFmpeg setup dialog instead of only stopping the download
ui-controller:F5.problem: Assigning `CancelButton = _cancel` makes WinForms set _cancel.DialogResult = DialogResult.Cancel, because the button's DialogResult was None. Button.OnClick then sets the form's DialogResult to Cancel before OnCancelClicked runs. The modal loop raises FormClosing. OnFormClosing cancels it while busy but sets _closeWhenIdle = true, so the DownloadAsync finally block (line 157) calls Close() as soon as the cancellation completes. The intended behaviour (the comment at line 89 says "Esc: stops a running download, otherwise closes", and the status says "Download stopped. You can start it again whenever you like.") never happens.
ui-controller:F5.failure_scenario: On first run the user starts the 100 MB download, sees it is slow, and presses "Stop download" so they can use "I have it - browse..." instead. The dialog disappears, SetupFfmpegAsync treats it as a cancel, and the user lands back on the main window with the "needs FFmpeg" banner. The stop message is never shown and the Browse button never becomes available.
ui-controller:F5.verified_fix: Right after `CancelButton = _cancel;` add `_cancel.DialogResult = DialogResult.None;`. OnCancelClicked already sets DialogResult = Cancel when idle, and Esc still routes through PerformClick -> OnCancelClicked, which then only stops the download. The _closeWhenIdle path in OnFormClosing then only runs for title-bar X or Alt+F4, which is the intended case.

ui-controller:F6.title: Double-clicking Record starts and immediately stops a recording, and a queued Record press makes the "press again" advice wrong
ui-controller:F6.problem: FlatButton derives from Button, which turns off StandardDoubleClick, so a double-click raises Click twice. ToggleRecordingAsync has no debounce. With the buffer running, the first click calls _engine.StartRecording() synchronously and the second sees IsRecording and calls FinishRecordingAsync. With the buffer off, the second click (or hotkey press) shows "Replay is starting. Press Record again in a few seconds.", but the first request still starts the recording once the buffer is up. Pressing Record again as told then stops it. The Save buttons (HomeView.cs:135) have the same double-click issue and queue two identical saves.
ui-controller:F6.failure_scenario: A non-technical user double-clicks "● Record" on the Home page. The toasts read "Recording started" and then "Recording saved (00:02)", and nothing is being recorded. Or, with the buffer off, they click Record twice, follow the toast's "press Record again" advice, and that press ends the recording that had just started.
ui-controller:F6.verified_fix: In ToggleRecordingAsync, record the time of the last accepted toggle and ignore a toggle within about 600 ms (or ignore a stop within 1 s of a start). Add a _recordStartPending flag set while a Record-initiated StartReplayAsync is in progress. While it is set, a further press should say "Recording will start as soon as the replay is on" (or cancel the pending start) instead of "press Record again". In SaveLast(seconds), ignore a request of the same length within about 1 s of the previous one.

ui-controller:F7.title: "Replay on" toast advertises a save hotkey that is cleared or not working ("Not set saves the last 15 min")
ui-controller:F7.problem: onText is built unconditionally as `$"Replay on - {HotkeyText.Describe(_settings.SaveReplayHotkey)} saves the last ..."`. When the user cleared the save hotkey, Describe returns "Not set". When registration failed (for example because another app took the combination, which is in _hotkeyErrors), the toast still names the key as if it works. This toast is shown for every hotkey start and for every Launch start while the window is hidden, which is the common "Start with Windows" case.
ui-controller:F7.failure_scenario: A user clears the save hotkey and enables Start with Windows. At every logon the overlay reads "Replay on - Not set saves the last 15 min". Or Ctrl+Alt+F9 is taken by another tool: the toast promises Ctrl+Alt+F9 saves a clip, the user presses it in-game, and nothing happens.
ui-controller:F7.verified_fix: Build the text conditionally: if _settings.SaveReplayHotkey?.IsAssigned == true and !_hotkeyErrors.ContainsKey(HotkeyAction.SaveReplay), keep the current wording. Otherwise use "Replay on - save clips from the tray menu" (or plain "Replay on").

spec-completeness:F1.title: A resolution or refresh-rate change during a resume deletes the whole buffer (README says it is kept)
spec-completeness:F1.problem: Every supervised restart re-reads the monitors and re-resolves the settings (AppController.StartReplayAsync line 795, then BuildConfig/QualityMath.Resolve). With Resolution=Native (the default), the output size follows the monitor's current mode, and EffectiveFps follows its current refresh rate. Both are part of CaptureConfig.Signature (Models.cs:108). Once the new run is added, CompatibleRunsNewestFirst no longer includes the older runs, and JanitorTick calls DeleteExpired(-inf) on them within 2 s. All unpinned footage from before the switch is deleted. README line 46 says the opposite ('a game switching resolution/fullscreen ... PC Clipper resumes by itself and keeps what it had already buffered'). While resuming, HomeView:247 also tells the user 'Your last 12:34 is kept and can still be saved' just before it is deleted.
spec-completeness:F1.failure_scenario: Desktop at 2560x1440, Resolution=Native, buffer 60 min. The user plays CS2 in exclusive fullscreen at 1280x960 for 40 min. On game start, ddagrab gets ACCESS_LOST and the restart resolves 1280x960, so the earlier desktop footage is deleted. After a great round the user alt-tabs to PC Clipper and clicks 'Save last 5 min'. The mode switches back to 2560x1440, ffmpeg dies, the restart creates a new signature, and the janitor deletes all 40 min of game footage about 2 s after the new run starts. The save contains only the seconds since the alt-tab. A game that only switches the monitor to 60 Hz while 120 fps is chosen does the same.
spec-completeness:F1.verified_fix: (1) AppController.BuildConfig: for StartKind.Resume when _engine.ActiveConfig is not null and has the same Monitor.DeviceName, Vendor and Codec, keep the previous run's Width, Height, Fps and BitrateKbps so the Signature stays the same. Add settable Width, Height and BitrateKbps to CaptureConfigBuilder for this. VideoGraph already inserts scale_d3d11 (NVIDIA/AMD) or vpp_qsv/scale_d3d11 (Intel/CPU) when cfg.Width/Height differ from the new Monitor.Width/Height, so frames get rescaled to the session's canvas. Letterboxing a different aspect ratio is optional. (2) As a safety net in ReplayEngine.JanitorTick, stop calling DeleteExpired(-inf) on incompatible runs. Age them out by wall-clock time against BufferSeconds and let SaveLastAsync save the newest incompatible group as a separate file, or at least tell the user the buffer was reset. (3) Fix README line 46 and the HomeView 'is kept' text if a reset can still happen.

spec-completeness:F2.title: A long recording is lost when the buffer drive fills, because the auto-save needs the same space again and then the pins are released
spec-completeness:F2.problem: Recording length is 'unlimited (disk permitting)': pinned segments grow in the buffer folder until JanitorTick's guard (line 454) sees less than 2 GB free. It then kills capture as a non-retryable fault. AppController.OnEngineProblem (line 1006) then calls FinishRecordingAsync, which concatenates the whole recording into the clips folder. With the defaults, the buffer is in %LOCALAPPDATA% and the clips are in Videos, both on C:. That concat needs as many bytes again but only about 2 GB are free, so it fails with 'the clips drive is full'. StopRecordingAsync's finally then runs rec.Dispose() (line 594), which releases the pins. The session is still alive in the Faulted state with the janitor running, so on the next tick everything older than BufferMinutes is deleted.
spec-completeness:F2.failure_scenario: C: has 50 GB free, 4K60 HEVC High (about 74 Mbps, about 33 GB/h), buffer 60 min, default folders. The user starts a recording and plays for 1.5 h. About 48 GB of pinned segments reach the 2 GB limit, and the replay stops with 'Drive C: is almost full'. The automatic save needs about 48 GB more and fails, the toast says 'Saving failed: the clips drive is full.', and 2 s later every segment but the last 60 min is deleted. The 1.5-hour recording is gone, with no chance to free space and retry.
spec-completeness:F2.verified_fix: (1) In ReplayEngine.StopRecordingAsync, call rec.Dispose() only when the save succeeds. On failure, keep the Recording (and its pins) in a _failedRecording slot. Expose RetryFailedRecordingAsync(string outputMp4) and DiscardFailedRecording(), and have AppController offer 'Save recording to another folder…'. (2) Before ConcatAsync, sum the selected segments' FileInfo.Length and compare it with GetFreeBytes(output folder), plus 2 GB when it is on the buffer volume. Fail fast with a clear message and do not release the pins. (3) While a recording runs and the clips folder is on the buffer's volume, stop the recording itself (not the buffer) once free < pinnedRecordingBytes + 2 GB, while there is still room to write it. Warn at a softer threshold.

spec-completeness:F3.title: The start-time space check ignores clip output, and saving onto the buffer drive trips the 2 GB guard and stops the replay
spec-completeness:F3.problem: CheckFreeSpace only requires bufferBytes + 2 GB, and ConcatAsync never checks free space on the clips drive. By default both folders are on C:. Once the buffer is full, free space is about the 2 GB headroom plus whatever was spare. Each saved clip then takes free space permanently, and while a save writes its .part file, the every-10-s guard in JanitorTick (lines 451-461) sees less than 2 GB and kills capture as NOT retryable. The save itself then runs out of space and fails. The user ends up with no clip and no replay, so the footage they wanted is no longer being kept.
spec-completeness:F3.failure_scenario: 1440p60 High, 60-min buffer (about 17.6 GB). C: has 25 GB free, so the start check passes (needs about 19.6 GB). After an hour the user presses '1 hour'. About 5 GB into writing 'Clip ... .mp4.part', the guard stops the replay ('Drive C:\ is almost full ... replay buffer was stopped'), the save then fails with 'the clips drive is full', and the .part file is deleted. Even with more space, saving a few 15-min clips over an evening hits the same guard.
spec-completeness:F3.verified_fix: In SaveLastAsync, after selecting and pinning, compute need = Σ new FileInfo(seg.Path).Length (+1% for MP4 overhead). If the clips path is on the same volume as BufferRoot (compare Path.GetPathRoot of the full paths), require free ≥ need + MinFreeBytesWhileRunning, otherwise free ≥ need + a small margin. If not, return SaveResult.Fail($"Not enough space on {drive} to save {len} (needs {FormatBytes(need)}, {FormatBytes(free)} free). Free up space or pick another clips folder in Settings.") without starting ffmpeg. Optionally pass GetFreeBytes(ClipsFolder) into the Settings estimate line ('saving 1 hour needs about X GB more').

spec-completeness:F4.title: The encoder fallback picks another GPU's encoder, which cannot read the capture GPU's frames, instead of falling back to CPU
spec-completeness:F4.problem: FfmpegProbe tests encoders with software lavfi frames, so an encoder on any GPU counts as working. Capture always runs on the monitor's adapter (-init_hw_device d3d11va=dda:{Monitor.AdapterIndex}, FfmpegCommandBuilder.cs:94). For NVIDIA and AMD, the D3D11 frames go to the encoder with no conversion (zero copy), and Intel uses hwmap=derive_device=qsv. Frames from adapter A cannot be encoded by vendor B's encoder. ResolveVendor nevertheless returns 'any working hardware encoder' (lines 150-151) when the monitor GPU's encoder does not work, and it honours an explicit vendor choice for a monitor on another GPU. The Settings dropdown labels those vendors as working. The docs/research notes say exactly this ('Hybrid laptops ... break zero-copy ... pick QSV/AMF ... or the download path').
spec-completeness:F4.failure_scenario: A desktop with an RTX card driving the monitor, NVIDIA driver 560 (NVENC needs 570+, so all *_nvenc fail the probe) and a Ryzen 7000 iGPU, which is enabled by default (h264_amf works in the probe). Auto resolves AMD, and AMF receives D3D11 textures from the NVIDIA device, so the replay never starts. The message is generic or misleading (AMF/'update your AMD driver'), although libx264 would work. Laptop variant: the internal panel is on the Intel iGPU and the user picks 'NVIDIA'. NVENC fails with 'OpenEncodeSessionEx failed: unsupported device', which Explain() maps to 'The NVIDIA encoder is busy...', and it is RETRYABLE, so Launch/Resume keep retrying.
spec-completeness:F4.verified_fix: In QualityMath.ResolveVendor, map monitorGpuVendorId to fromGpu. When fromGpu is known (≠ Auto), return a hardware vendor only if it equals fromGpu and VendorWorks(fromGpu). Otherwise return Cpu, both for Auto and when an explicit cross-GPU vendor is requested (Warnings already reports '<X> encoder did not work on this PC; using CPU'). Keep the 'any working vendor' loop only when the monitor's vendor is unknown (GpuVendorId == 0, the Screen.AllScreens fallback). Cross-GPU encoding can come later via WGC plus -init_hw_device cuda/qsv on the encoder's adapter, as the research describes. In SettingsView.RelabelEncoders, label a vendor that differs from monitor.GpuVendorId 'not for this monitor'. In ReplayEngine.Explain, check 'unsupported device' before the 'OpenEncodeSessionEx failed' rule and return a non-retryable 'This encoder is on a different graphics chip than this monitor…' message.

spec-completeness:F5.title: With no working GPU encoder, Auto records with libx265 (CPU HEVC) at native resolution, and the user is never told why
spec-completeness:F5.problem: ResolveCodec tries HEVC first for every vendor, including CPU, where 'works' means only 'compiled in'. When no hardware encoder passes the probe, a common case being an NVIDIA driver below 570 with these FFmpeg builds, Auto becomes libx265 -preset veryfast at native resolution and 60 fps. That costs several times more CPU than libx264. The probe's stderr ('required nvenc API version' / driver too old) is only logged. The Home page shows nothing, and the Settings warning just says 'No GPU encoder found'.
spec-completeness:F5.failure_scenario: First run on a GTX 1660 or RTX 3060 with a 2024 driver and a 1440p monitor. The NVENC probes fail, and replay auto-starts with HEVC (CPU) 2560x1440 60 fps. The game stutters, speed drops below 1, and ffmpeg falls behind. Audio gets choked until the 60 s PCM queue overflows and the run restarts, so clips are choppy. Nothing tells the user that updating the NVIDIA driver would fix it, and the Home page only shows 'HEVC (H.265) (CPU)' in small text.
spec-completeness:F5.verified_fix: In ResolveCodec, when vendor == EncoderVendor.Cpu and requested == Auto, try H264 first (order H264, HEVC, AV1); HEVC stays automatic only when width > 4096. Optionally, in Resolve, cap Auto+CPU to 1080p and 60 fps when s.Resolution == Native. In FfmpegProbe, keep the failure tail per hardware encoder in caps (for example a FailureReasons dictionary). When the monitor's vendor encoder failed with an NVIDIA driver-version message, show a Home banner or toast once: 'Your NVIDIA driver is too old for its video encoder (needs 570 or newer). Update it to record without slowing your game.'

spec-completeness:F6.title: The automatic switch to Windows Graphics Capture ignores the Windows 10 yellow border and stays on for the rest of the session
spec-completeness:F6.problem: The SPEC says Auto uses WGC only above 60 fps on Windows 11, because Windows 10 draws an undisableable yellow border. MaybeSwitchCaptureMethod and BuildConfig (lines 887-904) only check WgcPossible (gfxcapture present and an HMONITOR), not QualityMath.IsWindows11. Two quick DDA start failures are enough, and a UAC prompt or Win+L that stays up about 3-4 s produces them: the run dies (healthy), then the restarts after 1 s and 2 s fail on the secure desktop. _methodOverride is never cleared when capture becomes healthy again (SuperviseTick 1121-1131 and RegisterFailure leave it), so WGC stays until the user turns replay off or changes settings. QualityMath.Warnings only warns in the Settings preview, not for this runtime override.
spec-completeness:F6.failure_scenario: Windows 10 22H2, defaults (Auto, 60 fps). During a game the user locks the PC for a minute, or reads a UAC prompt for 5 s. After it closes, capture resumes with gfxcapture, and a yellow border is drawn around the monitor over the game for the rest of the session with no explanation. On Windows 11 the same switch silently brings in WGC's static-screen problems (see F7).
spec-completeness:F6.verified_fix: In MaybeSwitchCaptureMethod, add `&& QualityMath.IsWindows11` to the DDA→WGC condition. Make the override one-shot: in SuperviseTick's healthy branch (or when a run started with the override reaches HealthyRun), set `_methodOverride = null`, so the next interruption tries Desktop Duplication again. While the override is active, show a quiet detail line ('Using Windows Graphics Capture after repeated interruptions').

spec-completeness:F7.title: With Windows Graphics Capture the replay cannot start on a still screen, and it restarts over and over when the screen stays still for over a minute with audio on
spec-completeness:F7.problem: gfxcapture in FFmpeg 8.1 sends no frames while nothing changes. The fps filter needs a second frame before it outputs anything, so no 2-s segment is completed. LaunchRunAsync still requires a completed segment within 20 s ('No video arrived within 20 seconds (is the monitor asleep?)'), with no exemption for WGC. Explain() then maps this to 'The video engine stopped unexpectedly (code -1)', which is retryable. While running, a still WGC screen also stops ffmpeg reading the audio pipe (scheduler choke). After 60 s the QueuedPcmSink (QueuedPcmSink.cs:39-41) overflows, the pump faults, and the run is killed. Each restart then fails again until something moves, with backoff up to 30 s. WGC is the Auto choice for 120 fps on Windows 11, the headline quality option.
spec-completeness:F7.failure_scenario: Windows 11, 144 Hz monitor, 120 fps, 'Start with Windows' and 'Turn replay on when PC Clipper starts'. At login the desktop is still, so 6 start attempts fail and the toast says 'Replay couldn't start: The video engine stopped unexpectedly (code -1). (No video arrived within 20 seconds...)'. Or: the user leaves a paused game menu for 2 minutes. Capture restarts, every start fails, a 'Replay keeps getting interrupted' toast appears, and when play resumes the first 30+ s are not captured while the backoff runs.
spec-completeness:F7.verified_fix: In LaunchRunAsync, when cfg.Method == WindowsGraphicsCapture, count the run as started once the anchor line has arrived (run.AnchorTimestamp != 0, meaning the first frame passed through the graph) or progress shows frame > 0, with ffmpeg still alive. Do not require a completed segment, and drop or extend the 20 s 'No video' timeout for WGC. For the audio overflow on WGC runs, do not fault: in QueuedPcmSink, discard the oldest queued audio on overflow instead of throwing (A/V alignment of the stalled stretch does not matter because no video exists for it), or raise the cap for WGC. The real fix is for gfxcapture to produce frames continuously: use dup_frames once a build that has it (FFmpeg master after 9.1) is pinned, or keep frames flowing another way until then.

spec-completeness:F8.title: The H.264 width cap uses a 2160p height, which keeps ultrawide outputs above 4096 px (and upscales them)
spec-completeness:F8.problem: When only H.264 works and the width is above 4096, Resolve 'caps' the size with TargetSize(P2160, monitor). For any aspect ratio wider than about 1.9:1 this does not reduce the width below 4096, and it even raises the height above native.
spec-completeness:F8.failure_scenario: A 5120x1440 super-ultrawide, or 3440x1440 with the 4K/5K preset, on a GPU or iGPU where only h264 works. The cap yields 7680x2160 or 5160x2160, which the hardware H.264 encoder rejects, so the replay fails with 'encoder can't handle these settings' although 4096x1152 would have worked.
spec-completeness:F8.verified_fix: Replace the cap with an aspect-preserving fit: `double k = Math.Min(1.0, Math.Min((double)H264MaxWidth / w, 4096.0 / h)); w = (int)(w * k) & ~1; h = (int)(h * k) & ~1;`, applied to the already-computed (w, h). Never go above the native height: also clamp k so h ≤ monitor.Height.

spec-completeness:F9.title: Turning off, exiting or applying settings during a long save silently kills or corrupts the save
spec-completeness:F9.problem: TearDownSessionAsync waits at most 2 min for in-flight saves and then deletes the session folder. ExitAsync gives engine.StopAsync only 30 s (AppController:1787) and then exits, and the job object kills the concat ffmpeg. The user gets no warning that a save is running. A killed save leaves a 'Clip ... .mp4.part' file that is never cleaned up. For multi-run (after any UAC interruption) or AV1 saves, the concat demuxer opens later files only when it reaches them, so deleting the folder after 2 min removes files the save still needs.
spec-completeness:F9.failure_scenario: On an HDD the user presses '1 hour' (a multi-minute copy), then picks Exit from the tray. 30 s later the app quits, the clip is lost and a stray .part file is left in Videos\PC Clipper. Or they press Turn OFF / Test my PC / apply settings: after 2 min the folder is deleted mid-save and the save fails with 'Saving failed. Details are in the log'.
spec-completeness:F9.verified_fix: In AppController, keep the save Tasks (not just the counts) in a list. In ExitAsync, StopReplayAsync (and therefore RestartReplayAsync and TestPcAsync) await them before calling _engine.StopAsync, showing 'Saving clip…' and, on exit, offering Wait / Cancel. In TearDownSessionAsync, remove the fixed 2-minute cut-off, or cancel saves explicitly through a session CancellationToken passed to ConcatAsync so they fail cleanly and delete their .part. At startup, delete stale '*.mp4.part' files in the clips folder older than a few minutes.

spec-completeness:F10.title: Changing only the buffer length clears the buffer, although nothing in the capture changes
spec-completeness:F10.problem: CaptureDiffers includes BufferMinutes, so the confirm dialog and StopAsync+StartAsync wipe the buffer. BufferSeconds is not part of the stream signature, and the engine already supports changing it while keeping the buffer (StartAsync sets session.BufferSeconds on keepBuffer).
spec-completeness:F10.failure_scenario: The dimmed '1 hour' button's tooltip says 'Your buffer keeps 30 min. Increase it in Settings.' The user sets 60 min, Save asks to clear the buffer, and the last 30 min of gameplay they wanted to keep is deleted. Lowering the length to save disk space wipes the buffer the same way.
spec-completeness:F10.verified_fix: Remove BufferMinutes from CaptureDiffers. Add `public void SetBufferSeconds(int seconds)` to ReplayEngine, setting CurrentSession().BufferSeconds under _gate so the janitor picks it up next tick. When the length grows, run the CheckFreeSpace estimate against GetFreeBytes and warn instead of failing. Call it from ApplySettingsAsync when only BufferMinutes changed, with no confirmation and no restart.

spec-completeness:F11.title: The record hotkey is silently ignored while the previous recording is still being saved
spec-completeness:F11.problem: ToggleRecordingAsync returns at once with no toast or sound while _recordingSaving is true. Saving a long recording can take minutes, and in a game the hotkey is the only control.
spec-completeness:F11.failure_scenario: The user stops a 1-hour recording (the save takes several minutes on an HDD) and presses Ctrl+Alt+F10 again in-game to record the next match. Nothing happens and no notice appears, so they believe they are recording, but nothing is being recorded.
spec-completeness:F11.verified_fix: Simplest fix: replace the silent return with `if (_recordingSaving && !_engine.IsRecording) { Notify("Still saving your last recording - press Record again in a moment.", ToastKind.Info, SoundKind.Error); return; }`. Allowing a new recording while the old one saves is possible (the engine clears _recording at the start of StopRecordingAsync), but FinishRecordingAsync would then need its own task per recording instead of the single _recordingSaving/_recordingSaveTask pair.
